usage: 고양이 ends in a vowel, so the subject marker is 가, not 이
키우다 (to raise/keep a pet) is the natural verb, paired with object 를
animals are counted with 마리, never with 개 (which is for objects)
길 (street) + 고양이; a very common compound you will see on signs and news
examples: 고양이가 귀여워요.
The cat is cute.
simple: subject 가 + the high-frequency adjective 귀엽다
저는 고양이를 키우고 싶어요.
I want to keep a cat.
everyday: object 를 with 키우다 + -고 싶어요 'want to'
우리 고양이는 사람을 별로 안 좋아해요.

nuance: 고양이 is the plain, everyday noun for a cat, neutral in register and usable from the classroom to the news. There is no separate male/female word the way English has none either, so 고양이 covers them all. The pitfall for English speakers is the existence verb: you must say 고양이가 있어요 ('there is a cat'), because 있다 takes the subject particle 가/이 — English 'I have a cat' tempts learners to reach for an object and say the ungrammatical 고양이를 있어요. usage: 날다 (to fly) is the signature verb; subject marker 가 after the vowel
counted with the animal counter 마리
지저귀다 is the natural verb for small-bird song, more specific than 노래하다
examples: 나무에 새가 있어요.
There is a bird in the tree.
simple: location 에 + existence 있어요 with subject 가
아침마다 새가 지저귀어요.
Birds chirp every morning.
everyday: 마다 'every' + the verb 지저귀다 for birdsong
새 한 마리가 하늘을 날아요.
One bird is flying across the sky.
real situation: 하늘을 날다 'fly the sky' uses 을, an idiomatic exception
nuance: 새 is the one-syllable umbrella word for any bird, neutral and basic. To name a species Koreans prefix or attach another element — 참새 (sparrow), 까치 (magpie), 비둘기 (pigeon), 독수리 (eagle) — so 새 is the generic, the others are specific, much like 'bird' versus 'sparrow' in English. The big trap is the homophone 새 meaning 'new', which is a pre-noun (관형사) appearing before a noun, as in 새 가방 'new bag'; the bird stands alone as a full noun and can take particles, so 새가 noticeably differs in role from the adjectival 새. One sound point: when you fly somewhere, Korean idiomatically says 하늘을 날다 with the object particle 을 even though English 'fly in the sky' feels locative — treat 하늘을 날다 as a fixed expression rather than translating 'in' as 에서.

usage: 헤엄치다 (to swim) is the verb for fish/animals in water; subject 가
키우다 'to raise' an aquarium fish, with object 를
living fish are counted with 마리
잡다 'to catch' — the verb of fishing, takes object 를
examples: 어항에 물고기가 있어요.
There is a fish in the tank.
simple: 어항 (fish tank) + 에 + existence 있어요
저는 작은 물고기를 키워요.
I keep small fish.
everyday: adjective 작은 'small' modifying the object 물고기를
바다에서 물고기를 많이 잡았어요.
We caught a lot of fish in the sea.
real situation: 에서 marks the place of action, 잡다 + past 잡았어요

키우다 for keeping it as a pet, with object 를
counted with the animal counter 마리
처럼 'like'; a natural simile comparing speed
examples: 공원에 토끼가 있어요.
There is a rabbit in the park.
simple: 공원 (park) + location 에 + 있어요 with subject 가
아이가 토끼한테 풀을 줘요.
The child gives grass to the rabbit.
everyday: 한테 'to (an animate)' marks the rabbit as recipient

nuance: 토끼 is the plain noun for a rabbit or hare, learned by Korean children very early through songs and the famous legend of the 달토끼 ('moon rabbit') who pounds rice cakes (떡) on the moon — so the word carries a gentle, fairy-tale warmth. usage: 곰 ends in a consonant, so the subject marker is 이, not 가
counted with the animal counter 마리
곰 is a stock simile for someone clumsy or dim; 처럼 'like'
인형 (doll/stuffed toy); the standard word for a plush bear
examples: 동물원에 곰이 있어요.
There is a bear at the zoo.

곰이 겨울에 잠을 자요.
Bears sleep in winter.
everyday: 잠을 자다 'to sleep', with the seasonal 겨울에
저 사람은 진짜 곰 같아요.

Culturally 곰 anchors the Dangun foundation myth, where a bear becomes the mother of the Korean nation, and in casual speech calling someone 곰 같다 means they are dense, clumsy, or slow to catch on (the opposite of 여우 'fox', which implies cunning). usage: 무섭다 'scary/frightening' is the typical adjective; subject 가
counted with the animal counter 마리

everyday: adverb 정말 'really' + the adjective 무섭다

사자가 정말 커요.

말을 타다 'to ride a horse' is the fixed collocation; object 을
counted with the animal counter 마리
빠르다 'fast' (a 르 irregular) describes the horse; subject 이
examples: 농장에 말이 있어요.
There is a horse on the farm.

저는 말을 타고 싶어요.
I want to ride a horse.

꿈 'dream'; dreaming of a pig is an omen of money/luck
examples: 농장에 돼지가 있어요.
There is a pig on the farm.
simple: 농장 (farm) + 에 + existence 있어요
저는 돼지고기를 좋아해요.
I like pork.
everyday: the meat 돼지고기 (not the animal) as object 를
어젯밤에 돼지꿈을 꿨어요.
I dreamed of a pig last night.
real situation: 꿈을 꾸다 'to have a dream', past 꿨어요
nuance: 돼지 is the everyday noun for the animal pig, and the sharp distinction is that its meat is 돼지고기 (돼지 + 고기 'meat') — Korean systematically names meats this way (소고기 beef, 닭고기 chicken), so you keep 돼지 for the living animal and switch to 돼지고기 at the table or butcher. Culturally the pig is auspicious: a 돼지꿈 ('pig dream') is believed to foretell money or good fortune, and pig-head offerings appear at 고사 ceremonies. As an insult 돼지 can mean a glutton or someone overweight, so be careful applying it to people. The English-speaker pitfall is using 돼지 for the food: 돼지 먹고 싶어요 sounds like you want to eat a live pig — say 돼지고기 먹고 싶어요. 돼지 ends in a vowel, so it takes 가/를.

Spelling it 되지. The correct vowel is ㅙ: 돼지. (되지 is a verb ending, as in 안 되지 'no good'.)

usage: 닭이 울다 'the chicken/rooster crows'; subject 이 after the consonant cluster
counted with the animal counter 마리
고기 'meat'; the cooked/raw meat is 닭고기, the live bird is 닭
a famous dish; 닭 here names the chicken as the ingredient
examples: 농장에 닭이 있어요.
There is a chicken on the farm.
simple: 닭 takes 이, and the ㄺ cluster splits so 닭이 is pronounced [달기]
새벽에 닭이 울어요.
The rooster crows at dawn.
everyday: 새벽 'dawn' + 울다, the verb for a bird's call
닭 한 마리로 백숙을 만들었어요.
I made baeksuk with one whole chicken.
real situation: instrumental 로 'with', a whole-chicken dish
nuance: 닭 names the live chicken, hen, or rooster, and its meat is 닭고기 (닭 + 고기 'meat'). Pronunciation is the main hurdle: 닭 ends in the consonant cluster ㄺ, so alone it sounds like [닥], but before a vowel-initial particle the ㄹ-ㄱ split surfaces and 닭이 is pronounced [달기], 닭을 [달글] — this resyllabification trips up beginners. Particle-wise the final consonant means the subject is 이 (닭이), object 을 (닭을). Note the register split for food: while raw/cooked chicken is 닭고기 and dishes keep 닭 (닭갈비, 닭볶음탕), Korean-style fried chicken is the loanword 치킨, so ordering delivery you say 치킨 시키자 not 닭 시키자. A chick is 병아리, a distinct word, not 새끼 닭.

키우다 'to raise a pet', with object 를
counted with the animal counter 마리
산책 (walk); 강아지 산책시키다 'take the dog for a walk' is everyday
examples: 우리 집에 강아지가 있어요.
There is a puppy in our house.
simple: location 에 + existence 있어요 with subject 가
저는 강아지를 키우고 싶어요.
I want to get a puppy.
everyday: object 를 with 키우다 + -고 싶어요 'want to'
우리 강아지가 벌써 다섯 살이에요.
Our dog is already five years old.
real situation: a grown pet still called 강아지 out of affection
nuance: 강아지 literally means a puppy (the young of 개 'dog'), but in real Korean life it is the warm, default word people use for any beloved pet dog regardless of age — saying 우리 강아지 about a ten-year-old dog is completely normal and conveys affection, much like English 'puppy' or 'doggy' used fondly. The neutral, technical word for a grown dog is 개, which is what you use in formal writing, signs (개 조심 'beware of dog'), and breed talk; bare 개 can also sound blunt or even appear in insults (이 개 같은...), so 강아지 is the gentler everyday choice. As an endearment, calling a child 우리 강아지 means 'my little darling'. The English-speaker pitfall is register: in a report or formal context use 개, but in warm daily speech 강아지 is right. It ends in a vowel, so it takes 가/를.
